title: The grapes
subtitle: Two great grapes and two more

steps.title: Pinot Noir and Chardonnay
steps.body: Burgundy's two great grapes are Pinot Noir, for reds, and Chardonnay, for whites. Unlike Bordeaux, Burgundy rarely blends: each wine is usually a single grape from a single place. The idea is that the climat, not the blend, gives the wine its character.

steps.title: Aligoté and Gamay
steps.body: Aligoté, a sibling of Chardonnay, makes crisp, lemony whites; Bouzeron, in the Côte Chalonnaise, is its own appellation. Aligoté is the traditional base of the Kir, with blackcurrant liqueur. Gamay, banned from the Côte d'Or in 1395, grows mainly in Beaujolais, though it's allowed in some Burgundy blends like Coteaux Bourguignons.

steps.prompt: Match each grape to its role.
steps.explanation: Burgundy is a land of single grapes.

steps.body: Order a Kir in Burgundy and you'll get Aligoté with crème de cassis, named after Félix Kir, a mayor of Dijon.

steps.prompt: Why does Burgundy rarely blend grapes?
options: It aims to show the character of each climat
steps.explanation: A single grape lets the site speak.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Pinot Noir and Chardonnay are Burgundy's great grapes
Wines usually come from one grape and one place
Aligoté and Gamay play smaller roles
